Empirical Research Plan  
“Education and Health: Causal Evidence from Compulsory‐Schooling Laws (CSLs)”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Primary strategy: Two-stage least squares (2SLS) instrumental-variables (IV) design, where compulsory-schooling‐law–induced variation in years of schooling serves as the instrument.

Why IV?  
• Treatment (education) is continuous; the policy shock shifts the entire schooling distribution.  
• CSLs vary by state and birth cohort, supplying plausibly exogenous cross-cohort, within-state variation.  
• Exclusion restriction is more credible than parallel-trends DID because health is observed decades after the policy shock, and CSLs have no obvious direct health channel.

Supplement: Event-study/DID graphs (education and health around reform cohorts) to verify first-stage relevance and absence of pre-trends.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Edu_i  = completed years of schooling for individual i.

Instrument (“treated”)  
Z_i = 1 if individual i’s compulsory-schooling age (CSA) in her state of birth and birth cohort exceeded her 14th birthday; 0 otherwise.  
(Formally, CSA_st ≥ 15 & AgeLeaving_i < CSA_st)

Control group  
Individuals born in the same state just before the law change whose CSA ≤ 14.

Timing  
Event date = the first birth cohort fully exposed to the new CSA (we code exposure based on age 6—the typical school‐starting age—relative to the reform year).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Relevance – CSL reforms increased completed schooling.  
Plausibility: Well documented in historical education research; will be tested by first-stage F-statistic.

A2. Exclusion – CSLs affect later health only through schooling (no direct health channel).  
Plausibility: Laws targeted schooling, not health; we will adjust for coincident child-labor laws and state economic conditions.

A3. Monotonicity – No one reduces schooling because the minimum was raised.  
Plausibility: Reasonable; dropping out earlier than the minimum is illegal.

A4. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA) – One cohort’s CSL does not affect another’s health directly.  
Plausibility: Minimal spillovers expected.

A5. Sample retention – Mortality-linked data do not differentially attrit by treatment status conditional on controls.  
Plausibility: Evaluate by comparing pre-treatment covariates and attrition patterns.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Remedies
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Simultaneous policy changes (child-labor laws, public-health campaigns).  
Remedy: Control for state-by-year labor-law indicators, economic variables (manufacturing wages, unemployment) at age 14; include state-specific linear trends.

T2. Selective migration across states.  
Remedy: Classify exposure by state of birth, not state of residence; drop individuals who migrated before age 16 as a robustness check.

T3. Differential mortality before survey date (survivor bias).  
Remedy: Use NLMS mortality follow-ups from baseline age 25+; estimate cause-specific hazards; perform Lee bounds using pre-treatment covariates.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(ivreg)
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)

# 1. Load NHIS & CSL information -----------------------------------
nhis <- fread("nhis_individual.csv")         # individual health + edu
nlms <- fread("nlms_mortality.csv")          # mortality follow-up
csl  <- fread("state_csl_history.csv")       # CSA by state-year

# 2. Merge & construct variables -----------------------------------
# Birth cohort & exposure
nhis[, birth_year := year_of_birth]
nhis <- merge(nhis, csl,
              by.x = c("state_of_birth","birth_year"),
              by.y = c("state","cohort_year"),
              all.x = TRUE)                 # CSA_st

# Instrument: exposed if CSA > 14
nhis[, Z := as.integer(CSA_age > 14)]

# Years of schooling (treatment)
nhis[, educ := years_schooling]

# Outcomes
nhis[, good_health := as.integer(self_report_health %in% c("Excellent","Very good"))]
nhis[, died5yr := as.integer(time_to_death <= 5)]   # from NLMS merge

# Controls
nhis[, age := survey_year - birth_year]
controls <- c("sex","race_ethnicity","state_of_birth","birth_year")

# 3. Main 2SLS specification ---------------------------------------
# First stage
fs <- feols(educ ~ Z | state_of_birth + birth_year, data = nhis,
            cluster = ~state_of_birth)
summary(fs)

# Second stage
iv <- feols(good_health ~ 1 | state_of_birth + birth_year | educ ~ Z,
            data = nhis, cluster = ~state_of_birth)
summary(iv)

# 4. Robustness: drop migrants -------------------------------------
native <- nhis[moved_before16 == 0]
iv_native <- feols(good_health ~ 1 | state_of_birth + birth_year | educ ~ Z,
                   data = native, cluster = ~state_of_birth)
summary(iv_native)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Prior: One additional year of schooling  
• raises probability of reporting “good/very good/excellent” health by ≈ 2–3 percentage points;  
• lowers 10-year all-cause mortality hazard by ≈ 1–2 deaths per 1,000 individuals (age 40–60).  
Direction: Education improves health and survival.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV Design)
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)
C1: Strong first stage (F > 10) ................. 1  
C2: Exclusion restriction credible .............. 0.5  
C3: No endogenous migration ...................... 0.5  
C4: Monotonicity (no “defiers”) ................. 1  
C5: Correct clustering / inference .............. 1  

Total: 4/5 – design is credible but hinges on exclusion & migration assumptions.
